## Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Identify **Simpson's Paradox** and explain why aggregated data can show the opposite of what disaggregated data reveals
- Distinguish **confounders from mediators** and explain why the causal model determines which answer is correct
- Recognize the **Prosecutor's Fallacy** -- confusing the probability of evidence given a hypothesis with the probability of a hypothesis given evidence
- Apply **causal reasoning** to cross-country MNH comparisons, avoiding misleading aggregate statistics
- Use **ggplot2 in R** to visualize Simpson's Paradox with aggregated vs. stratified plots
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**Core Insight:** The same dataset can produce two completely opposite conclusions depending on how you slice it. Simpson's Paradox is not a statistical curiosity -- it is a real-world trap that has misled policymakers, scientists, and courts. The causal model tells you which answer to trust.
:::


# The Paradox {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Same data. Opposite conclusions.</span>


## The Setup: A Training Program Across Four Countries

Imagine you are evaluating a new **emergency obstetric care (EmOC) training program** for midwives and health workers across four East African countries: Ethiopia, Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania.

. . .

You have outcome data from facilities that received the training and facilities that did not.

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**The combined data across all four countries shows this:**

Facilities **with** training: maternal mortality ratio of **310 per 100,000** live births

Facilities **without** training: maternal mortality ratio of **285 per 100,000** live births

The training program appears to **increase** maternal deaths. Should we shut it down?
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Wait.** Before you cancel the program, look at each country separately...
:::


## The Reveal: Country-by-Country

::: {.example-block}
[Country-Level Results]{.example-label}

| Country | With Training | Without Training | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Ethiopia** | 380 per 100K | 420 per 100K | **-40** (better) |
| **Rwanda** | 210 per 100K | 250 per 100K | **-40** (better) |
| **Kenya** | 290 per 100K | 340 per 100K | **-50** (better) |
| **Tanzania** | 190 per 100K | 230 per 100K | **-40** (better) |
:::

. . .

The training **reduces** maternal mortality in **every single country**.

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Same data. Opposite conclusions.**

Combined: training looks harmful. Country by country: training helps everywhere. This is Simpson's Paradox.
:::


## How Is That Possible?

The secret is in **who gets trained**.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Countries with **higher baseline mortality** (more severe conditions, weaker health systems) received **more** training -- because they needed it most
- Ethiopia and Kenya have higher baseline MMR and received the bulk of training slots
- Rwanda and Tanzania have lower baseline MMR and received fewer training slots
- When you combine the data, the high-mortality countries **dominate** the training group, dragging the average up
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**The hidden third variable:** Baseline severity determines *both* who gets trained *and* what the outcomes look like. It is a **confounder** -- and ignoring it reverses the true effect.
:::


# How Aggregation Lies {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">The mechanics of the reversal</span>


## The Composition Effect

Here is a simplified version showing how the numbers work:

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.example-block}
[Aggregated (Misleading)]{.example-label}

| Group | Trained | Untrained |
|---|---:|---:|
| Deaths | 186 | 143 |
| Total births | 60,000 | 50,000 |
| **MMR** | **310** | **286** |

Training looks worse!
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.example-block}
[Where the trained facilities are]{.example-label}

| Country | % of Trained | Baseline MMR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ethiopia | 40% | Very high |
| Kenya | 30% | High |
| Rwanda | 18% | Moderate |
| Tanzania | 12% | Lower |

Training is concentrated in hard places.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**The math of the reversal:** 70% of trained facilities are in high-mortality countries (Ethiopia + Kenya), but only 35% of untrained facilities are. The groups being compared are fundamentally different -- and the difference is driven by the confounder, not the treatment.
:::


## Visual: Combined vs. Separated

Think of it as two pictures of the same data:

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Picture 1: One Big Bar Chart**

You see two bars -- "Trained" vs. "Untrained." The trained bar is taller (worse). You conclude: training hurts.

But you are comparing apples to oranges. The trained group is full of facilities in the hardest settings.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Picture 2: Four Side-by-Side Charts**

You see the same comparison *within* each country. In every single chart, the trained bar is shorter (better). Training helps.

Now you are comparing apples to apples.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Aggregation hides the confounder.** When a third variable affects both group membership and outcomes, combining groups can flip the direction of the effect. The only way to see the truth is to **separate the groups**.
:::


## The Confounder in the DAG

The causal structure that generates Simpson's Paradox is the **fork** -- a confounder that is a common cause of both the treatment and the outcome:

. . .

<table style="width: 85%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node confounder">Baseline<br>Severity</div>
</td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8601; [+]</span>
</td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8600; [+]</span>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment">Training<br>Received</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8594; [-]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Maternal<br>Mortality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **Baseline Severity → Training:** Countries with worse outcomes receive more training (they need it most)
- **Baseline Severity → Mortality:** Countries with worse baselines have higher mortality regardless of training
- **Training → Mortality:** Training *actually reduces* mortality (the true causal effect is negative)
- The spurious positive association in aggregated data comes from the **back-door path** through Baseline Severity
:::


# UC Berkeley Admissions {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">The most famous example of Simpson's Paradox</span>


## The Lawsuit That Wasn't

In 1973, UC Berkeley was accused of gender discrimination in graduate admissions. The aggregated data looked damning:

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[Overall Admission Rates (Fall 1973)]{.example-label}

| | Applicants | Admitted | Rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Men** | 8,442 | 3,738 | **44%** |
| **Women** | 4,321 | 1,494 | **35%** |

A 9 percentage point gap. Women seemed to face a clear disadvantage.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**On the surface:** This looks like systematic bias against women. Lawyers filed a discrimination lawsuit.
:::


## But Then They Looked by Department

::: {.example-block}
[Department-Level Admission Rates]{.example-label}

| Department | Men Applied | Men Admit | Women Applied | Women Admit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 825 | 62% | 108 | **82%** |
| B | 560 | 63% | 25 | **68%** |
| C | 325 | 37% | 593 | **34%** |
| D | 417 | 33% | 375 | **35%** |
| E | 191 | 28% | 393 | **24%** |
| F | 373 | 6% | 341 | **7%** |
:::

. . .

In four out of six departments, **women were admitted at equal or higher rates** than men.

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**The paradox:** Women appeared disadvantaged overall, but were advantaged in most individual departments. Department choice was the confounder.
:::


## The Berkeley DAG

<table style="width: 85%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment rect">Gender</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8594;</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node confounder rect">Department<br>Applied To</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8594;</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome rect">Admission<br>Decision</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **Gender → Department:** Women disproportionately applied to departments with low admission rates (like English and Humanities), while men applied to departments with high rates (like Engineering)
- **Department → Admission:** Some departments admit 60%+ of applicants; others admit fewer than 10%
- The **overall gap** is driven by application patterns, not by discrimination within departments
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**But wait -- is Department a confounder or a mediator?** This is where the causal model becomes essential. If gender *causes* department choice, then Department is technically a mediator. The correct analysis depends on the question you are asking. We will return to this distinction in the next section.
:::


# The Causal Key {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Confounder vs. mediator: the same variable can play different roles</span>


## The Critical Distinction

::: {.definition-box}
**The same variable can be a confounder in one causal model and a mediator in another.** The DAG -- not the data -- tells you which role it plays. And that role determines whether you should adjust for it or not.
:::

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**CONFOUNDER (Common Cause)**

Treatment ← **Confounder** → Outcome

The confounder causes *both* the treatment and the outcome. It creates a spurious association.

[Adjust for it -- conditioning removes the bias]{.good-example}
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**MEDIATOR (On the Causal Path)**

Treatment → **Mediator** → Outcome

The mediator is *part of how* the treatment produces its effect.

[Do NOT adjust for it -- conditioning blocks the real effect]{.bad-example}
:::
:::
:::


## Confounder Example: Baseline Severity

In the EmOC training example, **Baseline Severity** is a confounder:

. . .

<table style="width: 75%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node confounder">Baseline<br>Severity</div>
</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8601;</span>
</td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8600;</span>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment">EmOC<br>Training</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8594; [-]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Maternal<br>Mortality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

- Baseline severity is *not caused by* the training -- it existed before the program started
- It influences who gets trained *and* what outcomes look like
- **We should adjust for it** to see the true effect of training

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Result:** When we stratify by baseline severity (i.e., look within each country), the confounding disappears and we see training's true benefit.
:::


## Mediator Example: Skill Level

Now consider a different variable -- **Skill Level after training:**

. . .

<table style="width: 75%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment">EmOC<br>Training</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8594; [+]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node">Skill<br>Level</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8594; [-]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Maternal<br>Mortality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

- Training *causes* improved skills, and improved skills *cause* lower mortality
- Skill Level is *on the causal path* -- it is the mechanism through which training works
- **We should NOT adjust for it** -- doing so would block the causal pathway and make training look ineffective

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**The danger of adjusting for a mediator:** If we compare trained and untrained facilities *among those with the same skill level*, we have removed the very effect we are trying to measure. Training would appear to do nothing -- because we controlled away its mechanism.
:::


## The Decision Rule

::: {.key-takeaway}
**The causal model settles the debate.**

The data alone cannot tell you whether to adjust for a variable. You need to know the **causal structure** -- is this variable a confounder (common cause) or a mediator (on the pathway)?

- **Confounder?** Adjust for it. Stratify. Condition on it.
- **Mediator?** Leave it alone. Do not condition on it.

Get this wrong, and you can reach exactly the wrong conclusion.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**This is why we spent Chapters 2-5 building causal models.** Without a DAG, Simpson's Paradox is unresolvable -- the data is genuinely consistent with both stories. The causal structure is what breaks the tie.
:::


# MNH Application: Comparing Countries {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Why raw country comparisons mislead</span>


## Maternal Mortality Across East Africa

Here are the most recent WHO/UNICEF estimates of the **maternal mortality ratio** (deaths per 100,000 live births) for the four countries in our study:

. . .

| Country | MMR (per 100K) | Annual Births (approx.) | Health System Context |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Ethiopia** | ~267 | ~3.3 million | Rapidly expanding but low baseline coverage |
| **Rwanda** | ~248 | ~370,000 | Strong community health system, small population |
| **Kenya** | ~342 | ~1.5 million | Mixed urban/rural, wide variation |
| **Tanzania** | ~238 | ~2.1 million | Moderate system strength, large rural population |

*Source: WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, World Bank, and UN Population Division estimates*

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Notice the variation.** Kenya has the highest MMR despite having a relatively strong urban health infrastructure. Tanzania has the lowest despite a large rural population. These differences reflect dozens of underlying factors -- and they make naive country comparisons treacherous.
:::


## The Naive Comparison Trap

Suppose a program runs EmOC training in all four countries. After two years, we measure the reduction in MMR:

. . .

::: {.example-block}
[Raw Cost-Effectiveness Comparison]{.example-label}

| Country | MMR Reduction | Program Spending | Apparent Efficiency |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Tanzania** | -22 points | $4.5M | Looks best |
| **Rwanda** | -19 points | $3.8M | Looks good |
| **Ethiopia** | -15 points | $12.0M | Looks worst |
| **Kenya** | -18 points | $7.2M | Looks mediocre |
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**Tempting conclusion:** "Tanzania gets the best results for the money. Shift spending away from Ethiopia."

**Why this is wrong:** Ethiopia's lower apparent efficiency reflects its *harder starting conditions* -- larger population, lower baseline coverage, weaker infrastructure. The same dollar buys less *visible* improvement, but may save more lives at the margin because the unmet need is so much larger.
:::


## The Confounder: Baseline Health System Strength

::: {.definition-box}
**Baseline burden** (MMR, health system capacity, population size, geographic access) is the confounder. It determines both where programs invest heavily *and* what raw outcomes look like. Ignoring it leads to Simpson's Paradox in cost-effectiveness rankings.
:::

. . .

<table style="width: 85%; margin: 0.4em auto; font-size: 0.55em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node confounder">Baseline<br>Burden</div>
</td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8601; [+]</span>
</td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow positive">&#8600; [+]</span>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node treatment">Program<br>Investment</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.3em;">
<span class="dag-arrow negative">&#8594; [-]</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.6em;">
<div class="dag-node outcome">Maternal<br>Mortality</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**The pattern is identical to our training example.** High-burden countries receive more investment *and* have worse outcomes. Without adjustment, the investment appears to cause worse outcomes -- when it actually causes better ones.
:::


## What Correct Adjustment Reveals

When we account for baseline burden -- comparing each country's outcomes to what would have been expected *without* the program, given its starting conditions:

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Naive Ranking:**

1. Tanzania (most efficient)
2. Rwanda
3. Kenya
4. Ethiopia (least efficient)

"Shift funds from Ethiopia to Tanzania."
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Adjusted Ranking:**

1. Ethiopia (highest marginal impact per dollar, given massive unmet need)
2. Kenya (large population, major gaps to address)
3. Tanzania (solid returns, nearing diminishing returns)
4. Rwanda (strong system already, less marginal gain)

"Ethiopia is where the next dollar saves the most lives."
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Rankings can reverse completely** when you adjust for the confounder. The country that looks least efficient on paper may be the best investment at the margin -- because it has the most room to improve.
:::


## The Lesson for Program Leaders

::: {.callout-box}
**Three rules for cross-country MNH comparisons:**
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
1. **Never compare raw cost-effectiveness across countries** without adjusting for baseline conditions. Different starting points make raw numbers incomparable.
2. **Always ask: what is the confounder?** In MNH, it is almost always some combination of baseline mortality burden, health system capacity, population size, and geographic access.
3. **Use the causal model to determine what to adjust for.** Baseline burden is a confounder (adjust for it). Quality improvement is a mediator (do not adjust for it). The DAG tells you which is which.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**This is not just about statistics.** Getting this wrong means shifting resources away from the countries that need them most -- and toward the countries that look good on paper because they started from a better position.
:::


# Bonus Insight: The Prosecutor's Fallacy {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">When a 99% accurate test does not mean a 99% chance</span>


## The Fallacy in One Slide

::: {.example-block}
[A Quick Thought Experiment]{.example-label}

A diagnostic test for a rare complication is **99% accurate** -- it correctly identifies the condition 99% of the time, and correctly rules it out 99% of the time.

You test positive.

**Question:** What is the probability you actually have the condition?
:::

. . .

Most people answer **99%**. That feels right -- the test is 99% accurate, after all.

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**The answer depends entirely on how rare the condition is.**

If the condition affects 1 in 1,000 people:

- Out of 100,000 people tested, **100** have the condition and **99** test positive (true positives)
- But **99,900** do NOT have it, and **999** of them test positive anyway (false positives)
- Total positive tests: 99 + 999 = **1,098**
- Chance you actually have it: 99 / 1,098 = **about 9%**

A "99% accurate" test gives you only a **9% chance** of actually having the condition.
:::


## Why This Matters

::: {.definition-box}
**The Prosecutor's Fallacy:** Confusing the probability of the evidence given the hypothesis with the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence. In plain language: confusing "how well the test works" with "what the test result means for you."
:::

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**What people hear:**

"The test is 99% accurate, so a positive result means 99% chance of disease."

This confuses P(positive | disease) with P(disease | positive).
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**What is actually true:**

"The probability of disease given a positive test depends on both the test accuracy **and** how common the disease is (the base rate)."

When the disease is rare, most positives are false positives.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**Connection to Simpson's Paradox:** Both fallacies share the same root cause -- ignoring a crucial piece of context (the confounder in Simpson's, the base rate in the Prosecutor's Fallacy). In both cases, the causal model tells you what context you need.
:::


# R Workshop {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Simulating and visualizing Simpson's Paradox with ggplot2</span>


## R Block 1: Simulate the Paradox

```{r}
#| label: simulate-simpsons
#| echo: true

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2024)

# Simulate an EmOC training program across 4 countries
# Confounder: country (determines both training allocation and baseline MMR)

simpsons_data <- tibble(
  country = c(
    rep("Ethiopia", 1200), rep("Kenya", 900),
    rep("Rwanda", 500),    rep("Tanzania", 400)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    # Confounder: high-burden countries get MORE training
    trained = case_when(
      country == "Ethiopia"  ~ rbinom(n(), 1, 0.70),
      country == "Kenya"     ~ rbinom(n(), 1, 0.60),
      country == "Rwanda"    ~ rbinom(n(), 1, 0.35),
      country == "Tanzania"  ~ rbinom(n(), 1, 0.25)
    ),
    # Outcome: training REDUCES mortality in every country
    # But high-burden countries have higher baseline mortality
    death_prob = case_when(
      country == "Ethiopia"  & trained == 1 ~ 0.038,
      country == "Ethiopia"  & trained == 0 ~ 0.052,
      country == "Kenya"     & trained == 1 ~ 0.029,
      country == "Kenya"     & trained == 0 ~ 0.041,
      country == "Rwanda"    & trained == 1 ~ 0.018,
      country == "Rwanda"    & trained == 0 ~ 0.025,
      country == "Tanzania"  & trained == 1 ~ 0.016,
      country == "Tanzania"  & trained == 0 ~ 0.022
    ),
    death = rbinom(n(), 1, death_prob),
    trained_label = ifelse(trained == 1, "Trained", "Not Trained")
  )

# Aggregated result (misleading)
simpsons_data |>
  group_by(trained_label) |>
  summarise(
    mortality_rate = mean(death),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Country-level result (correct)
simpsons_data |>
  group_by(country, trained_label) |>
  summarise(
    mortality_rate = mean(death),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = trained_label, values_from = c(mortality_rate, n))
```


## R Block 2: The Aggregated View (Misleading)

```{r}
#| label: plot-aggregated
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

library(ggplot2)

# Aggregated bar chart -- the misleading picture
p_aggregated <- simpsons_data |>
  group_by(trained_label) |>
  summarise(mortality_rate = mean(death), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trained_label, y = mortality_rate, fill = trained_label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", mortality_rate * 100)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Trained" = "#005CB9", "Not Trained" = "#FA7650")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.06)) +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregated: Training Appears HARMFUL",
    subtitle = "Combined across all four countries",
    y = "Mortality Rate", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#E24A3F", face = "bold")
  )

p_aggregated
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**If you stopped here, you would cancel a life-saving program.** The aggregated chart tells a false story because it mixes together countries with very different baselines.
:::


## R Block 3: The Stratified View (Correct)

```{r}
#| label: plot-stratified
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

# Stratified bar chart -- the true picture
p_stratified <- simpsons_data |>
  group_by(country, trained_label) |>
  summarise(mortality_rate = mean(death), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trained_label, y = mortality_rate, fill = trained_label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", mortality_rate * 100)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ country, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Trained" = "#005CB9", "Not Trained" = "#FA7650")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.07)) +
  labs(
    title = "Stratified: Training HELPS in Every Country",
    subtitle = "The same data, split by country",
    y = "Mortality Rate", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#3E9B6E", face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
  )

p_stratified
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**In every panel, the blue bar (Trained) is lower than the orange bar (Not Trained).** Training reduces mortality in every country. The aggregated chart lied because it mixed countries together without accounting for baseline severity.
:::


## R Block 4: Side-by-Side Comparison

```{r}
#| label: plot-combined
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 6

library(patchwork)

# Combine both views for maximum impact
(p_aggregated + p_stratified) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2.5)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Simpson's Paradox: Same Data, Opposite Conclusions",
    subtitle = "Left: aggregated (misleading) | Right: stratified by country (correct)",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", color = "#005CB9"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "#666")
    )
  )
```

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**This is the visualization you should remember from this chapter.** One dataset, two visualizations, opposite conclusions. The causal model tells you which one to trust.
:::


## R Block 5: The Regression Comparison

```{r}
#| label: regression-comparison
#| echo: true

# Naive regression: ignores the confounder (country)
naive_model <- lm(death ~ trained, data = simpsons_data)

# Adjusted regression: includes the confounder
adjusted_model <- lm(death ~ trained + country, data = simpsons_data)

# Compare the training coefficient
comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("Naive (ignores country)", "Adjusted (controls for country)"),
  Training_Effect = c(
    coef(naive_model)["trained"],
    coef(adjusted_model)["trained"]
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "Training appears to INCREASE mortality",
    "Training DECREASES mortality (correct)"
  )
)

print(comparison)

# The sign of the coefficient flips!
# Naive: positive (training looks harmful)
# Adjusted: negative (training is beneficial)
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**Key lesson:** The coefficient on `trained` literally changes sign when you add `country` to the regression. This is Simpson's Paradox expressed as **omitted variable bias** -- the statistical fingerprint of a missing confounder.
:::


## R Block 6: Visualizing the Confounder's Role

```{r}
#| label: plot-confounder
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Show how the confounder drives the paradox
# Plot: training rate vs. baseline mortality by country

country_summary <- simpsons_data |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(
    pct_trained = mean(trained),
    baseline_mortality = mean(death[trained == 0]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(country_summary, aes(x = pct_trained, y = baseline_mortality)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "#005CB9") +
  geom_text(aes(label = country), vjust = -1.2, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = "#FA7650") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.1, 0.85)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "The Confounder: Baseline Severity Drives Training Allocation",
    subtitle = "Countries with higher mortality receive more training -- creating the paradox",
    x = "Percentage of Facilities Trained",
    y = "Baseline Mortality Rate (Untrained Facilities)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#005CB9", face = "bold")
  )
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**This scatter plot shows why the paradox occurs.** Countries with higher baseline mortality (Ethiopia, Kenya) also have the highest training rates. When you aggregate, the high-mortality countries dominate the trained group, making training look harmful. The dashed line shows the positive correlation between severity and training -- the hallmark of the confounder.
:::


## Key Takeaways

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Simpson's Paradox** is not a curiosity -- it is a trap. Aggregated data can show the exact opposite of what is really happening. The same dataset, sliced two ways, gives two contradictory answers.

**The resolution is causal, not statistical.** The data alone cannot tell you which answer is correct. You need a causal model (a DAG) to identify whether a variable is a confounder (adjust for it) or a mediator (do not adjust).

**In MNH cost-effectiveness**, naive cross-country comparisons mislead because baseline burden is a confounder. Adjusting for it can reverse which countries and interventions look most effective -- and that reversal can save thousands of lives.
:::

Now that we understand how to correctly estimate causal effects (avoiding Simpson's Paradox), we turn to **making optimal decisions** with those estimates:

- **Influence diagrams** that add decision nodes to our causal models
- **Expected value** calculations for choosing between intervention options
- **Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI):** How much would it be worth to resolve uncertainty before investing?
- The critical difference between **observing** a variable and **intervening** on it (the do-operator in action)
:::

**The connection:** Chapter 6 taught us how to *correctly estimate* causal effects -- seeing through the paradox to the truth. Chapter 7 teaches us how to *use* those correct estimates to make the best possible investment decisions.
